country.name: Colombia
country.tagline: Equatorial Andean vineyards above 2,000 m in Boyacá, plus a tropical wine industry in the Cauca valley.

stats.note: FAOSTAT, official national figures: 3,003 ha of grapes in 2024, mostly table grapes in Valle del Cauca, and 2,272 t of wine in 2023. A 2026 travel survey counts about nine serious small wineries, while Casa Grajales in Valle del Cauca reports capacity of about 7 million litres a year

country.overview:
Colombia lies on the equator, so its vineyards have no winter. Two very different wine cultures have grown up anyway. In the tropical Cauca valley around La Unión, Valle del Cauca, the Grajales family has grown table and wine grapes for more than 40 years; their Casa Grajales winery, which reports a capacity of about 7 million litres a year, makes wines from grapes adapted to the tropics, harvested more than once a year, and runs the National Grape Park.

The quality scene is in the high Andes of Boyacá, north of Bogotá, around Villa de Leyva, Sutamarchán and Sáchica in the Alto Ricaurte at about 2,000 to 2,200 m, and in the Valle del Sol near Duitama and Nobsa at about 2,500 m. Cool nights, intense equatorial light and a dry, semi-desert microclimate let growers make Sauvignon Blanc, Riesling, Pinot Noir and Cabernet. Viñedos Ain Karim, established in 1988 near Sutamarchán and the first to plant Sauvignon Blanc in Colombia, and Marqués de Puntalarga in Nobsa, which grows Pinot Noir and Riesling, are the pioneers. With no seasons, vines can be pruned to give two harvests a year. There is no appellation system; volumes are tiny and almost all is drunk at home.

history.title: Casa Grajales and tropical wine
history.text: The Grajales family develops tropical viticulture in La Unión, Valle del Cauca, producing wine from multiple harvests a year.

history.title: Ain Karim
history.text: Viñedos Ain Karim is established near Sutamarchán, Boyacá, and plants Colombia's first Sauvignon Blanc.

country.classification: Colombia has no wine appellation system.
country.climate_soils: Equatorial climate with no seasons; quality vineyards rely on altitude (about 2,000 to 2,600 m in Boyacá) for cool nights, and on the dry, semi-desert microclimate of the Alto Ricaurte around Villa de Leyva, with eroded, low-fertility soils. In the Cauca valley, tropical heat allows several harvests a year.

grapes.name: Sauvignon Blanc, Riesling
grapes.note: The main whites of Boyacá's high vineyards.

grapes.name: Tropical-adapted varieties (including Isabella and Moscatel)
grapes.note: In the Cauca valley for Casa Grajales.

sites.name: Viñedos Ain Karim
sites.text: Established in 1988 on the road from Villa de Leyva to Santa Sofía, near Sutamarchán in Boyacá, at about 2,000 m. Ain Karim planted Colombia's first Sauvignon Blanc and makes red, white and rosé wines from its own vineyards, aged in an underground cellar.

sites.name: Marqués de Puntalarga
sites.text: A vineyard in the Valle del Sol near Nobsa, Boyacá, at about 2,500 m, between Duitama and Belencito. It grows Pinot Noir and Riesling (made dry and sweet) and hosts the Valle del Sol Vid y Vino event each December.

sites.name: Casa Grajales and National Grape Park
sites.text: Colombia's pioneering commercial winery in La Unión, Valle del Cauca, founded more than 40 years ago by the Grajales family, with a reported capacity of around 7 million litres a year from tropical-adapted grapes. Its National Grape Park and grape and wine museum explain viticulture in the tropics.
